title: How to Finance Development When Foreign Aid Runs Short
gist: Traditional official development assistance has fallen from $223 billion in 2023 to an estimated $175 billion in 2025 and is projected at $152-160 billion by 2029, erasing a decade of growth, while the remaining capital shifts to bilateral, quid-pro-quo, geopolitically-driven channels. The system is bifurcating: middle-income countries can access loans, blended finance and capital markets, while low-income and fragile states stay dependent on flat grant volumes, and the proposed fixes run from AI-enabled domestic revenue mobilization to pushing multilateral development bank balance sheets past AAA-preserving limits.

insights.claim: Traditional official development assistance from the established donor base peaked at $223 billion in 2023, fell to an estimated $175 billion in 2025, and is projected to reach only $152-160 billion by 2029 — roughly the 2016 level at the start of the Sustainable Development Goal era.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: A ~30% structural cut in concessional public capital over six years reprices sovereign risk and funding availability across frontier markets; watch 2029 donor budget trajectories as the base case, not a tail scenario.
insights.quote: traditional ODA is expected to fall to between $152 billion and $160 billion by 2029, erasing roughly a decade of funding growth
insights.locator: The Traditional Aid Order Has Fractured

insights.claim: Even on the broadest definition — adding other official flows that support development but lack concessional terms — total development assistance from bilateral providers and EU institutions is projected to fall from $350 billion in 2023 to as low as $275 billion by 2029.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Broadening the definition of aid does not rescue the headline: roughly $75 billion of annual external flows disappears regardless of accounting treatment.
insights.locator: Expanding the historically strict definition of aid

insights.claim: The United States' share of the global aid pool is projected to fall from roughly 30% to approximately 22% by 2029, making its retreat the single largest driver of the contraction.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: US-dependent recipient countries and US-funded implementers face the sharpest funding cliff; the gap is a leading indicator of where sovereign distress and service collapse appear first.
insights.locator: At the center of this retreat is the United States

insights.claim: Canada, France, Germany, the Netherlands, and the United Kingdom are all cutting development budgets under their own fiscal pressures, so no traditional donor is positioned to backfill the American withdrawal.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Assume correlated, not offsetting, donor behavior — European fiscal consolidation and defense spending compound rather than cushion the US cut.
insights.locator: With other major donors, including Canada, France, Germany

insights.claim: EU institutions are increasing contributions while European bilateral donors retreat, and could become the single largest development donor by 2029 at an estimated $29 billion.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Brussels becomes the marginal price-setter for concessional terms and conditionality in Africa and the neighborhood — track EU budget cycles as the new center of gravity.
insights.quote: EU institutions are increasing their contributions and could become the single largest development donor by 2029, at an estimated $29 billion
insights.locator: Other donors will need to play an important role

insights.claim: Gulf States led by Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates have entered the top 15 donor list but supplied only $8.5 billion, or 3.5%, of global official development assistance in 2024, and non-reporting powers add only a small further offset.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: The narrative that Gulf and non-Western capital replaces Western aid is quantitatively false at current volumes — do not underwrite deals on that assumption.
insights.locator: Meanwhile, reporting Gulf States, led by Saudi Arabia

insights.claim: Concentration among donors is falling — the top ten bilateral DAC country donors account for 52% of total development finance today, projected to drop to 44% by 2029 — which makes consensus harder because no single actor has the scale or mandate to set a common agenda.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Fragmentation raises transaction costs and coordination risk for anyone assembling multi-donor capital; it also removes the anchor that once made aid flows predictable.
insights.locator: While the top ten bilateral DAC country donors account for 52%

insights.claim: After half a century in which aid was driven mainly by poverty reduction and human development, bilateral donors are redirecting capital toward national security, trade, and migration objectives, turning development finance into economic statecraft with explicit quid pro quo terms.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Allocation now follows geopolitical alignment rather than need — screen exposure by a country's strategic value to donors, not by its development indicators.
insights.quote: Today, geopolitics has reasserted its dominance, with bilateral donors moving capital away from traditional development priorities toward a narrower set of national security, trade, and migration objectives.
insights.locator: A Shift from Soft Power to Economic Statecraft

insights.claim: Sweden is phasing out bilateral aid to several African countries and redirecting more than $1 billion to Ukraine, with other Nordic countries likely to follow as defense priorities displace human development programs.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: A concrete template for the reallocation: European defense and Ukraine reconstruction budgets are funded partly out of African aid lines.
insights.locator: In Northern Europe, defense priorities are displacing

insights.claim: Grant commitments are being replaced by strategic investment vehicles: Japan's $1.5 billion TICAD9 pledge is framed explicitly as trade rather than aid, while the EU's Global Gateway and Italy's $5.9 billion Mattei Plan tie infrastructure finance to migration control, energy security, and access to critical raw materials.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Infrastructure and critical-minerals developers gain a new class of state-backed co-financiers whose conditions are commercial and political, not concessional.
insights.quote: Japan’s $1.5 billion TICAD9 pledge operates explicitly as “trade, not aid,”
insights.locator: Traditional donors are also replacing grant commitments

insights.claim: Sub-Saharan Africa, despite having the highest SDG gaps and being a focal point of global poverty, must now compete for development funding against the Indo-Pacific and Eastern Europe.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Expect the widest funding-versus-need gap in sub-Saharan Africa — a warning for local currency debt, social spending, and fragile-state exposure there.
insights.locator: As a result, despite having the highest SDG gaps

insights.claim: Bilateral funding hit a record 63% of total development flows in 2024 while capital channeled through multilateral and pooled mechanisms fell 31%, from a $38 billion peak in 2021 to $26 billion in 2024.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Pooled vehicles — global health funds, climate funds, replenishments — are the structurally shrinking part of the system and face the most acute replenishment risk.
insights.locator: A Growing Demand for Donor Control

insights.claim: When fiscal pressure forced budget cuts in 2025, donors protected bilateral commitments and let pooled funds absorb a disproportionate share of the reductions, showing that multilateral channels are the shock absorber of choice.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: In any future austerity round, model pooled-fund replenishments as the first casualty, not a pro-rata victim.
insights.locator: When fiscal pressures forced widespread budget cuts in 2025

insights.claim: The shift to bilateral channels imposes a hidden administrative tax: development organizations and recipient governments must manage many separate sovereign relationships, each with its own priorities, processes, conditions, planning cycles, and reporting, which absorbs scarce capacity and slows deployment.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Effective capital delivered per dollar pledged is falling even faster than headline volumes — coordination capacity becomes a real bottleneck on disbursement.
insights.locator: Development organizations must now manage more individual sovereign relationships

insights.claim: Blended finance volumes reached $18 billion in 2024, but 90% of transactions bypassed the poorest nations and went to middle-income countries instead, undercutting the assumption that institutional investment can offset falling public funding.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Blended finance is a middle-income asset class, not a low-income solution — discount any thesis that private capital mobilization closes the fragile-state gap.
insights.quote: blended finance volumes reached $18 billion in 2024, but 90% of transactions bypassed the poorest nations and flowed instead to middle-income countries
insights.locator: A Widening Two-Tier Financial System

insights.claim: Low-income countries still draw 80% of their inflows from grants, yet total grant volumes to them have been flat for over a decade, moving from 45 billion in 2011 to 43 billion in 2024 despite growing needs.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Real per-capita grant support has been eroding for years; the aid cuts land on a base that was already stagnant.
insights.locator: Low-income countries remain dependent on grants

insights.claim: Lower-middle-income countries saw their grant share fall from 46% to 33%, with debt filling the space, while upper-middle-income countries now receive on average 34 times the amount of other official flows that low-income countries do.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Capital is flowing to where it can be repaid, not where it is needed — a structural sorting that widens divergence between frontier and emerging sovereign credits.
insights.quote: Upper-middle-income countries now receive on average 34 times the amount of OOF as low-income countries.
insights.locator: A Widening Two-Tier Financial System

insights.claim: Substituting loans and non-concessional official flows for grants preserves near-term funding volumes but raises debt service burdens and restricts policy flexibility in countries already in or at high risk of debt distress.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Expect a rising wave of sovereign debt restructurings in low-income borrowers as grant-to-debt substitution compounds existing stress.
insights.quote: Although these instruments preserve near-term funding, they dramatically increase debt service burdens and place governments under severe and additional fiscal pressure.
insights.locator: The Structural Replacement of Grants with Debt

insights.claim: Domestic resource mobilization cannot replace lost aid in low- and middle-income countries, but it can stop the depletion of scarce public resources from weak collection, poor financial management, and leakage.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Calibrate expectations: tax reform is a leakage-reduction story, not a substitution story, so the external financing gap persists even with successful reform.
insights.locator: Expand domestic resource mobilization (DRM)

insights.claim: AI tools can reconcile fragmented tax and payment records, flag anomalous transactions, detect underpayment patterns, direct audits toward probable losses, and trace public money through government accounts, but the cost of AI remains a barrier to scaled deployment in many low- and middle-income countries.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: A concrete govtech demand pocket tied to falling inference costs and open-source models — donor-subsidized public-finance AI is an emerging procurement category.
insights.locator: AI makes that agenda more actionable

insights.claim: Some low sovereign ratings reflect incomplete information and limited local depth at rating agencies rather than genuine economic and political risk, so direct engagement with full liability disclosure can lower borrowing costs — a strategy Kenya and Nigeria already use.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: If mispricing from information gaps is real, frontier sovereign spreads in countries that improve disclosure offer a compression trade.
insights.quote: But some low ratings are a result of incomplete information and limited local depth by rating agencies.
insights.locator: Negotiate lower borrowing costs through stronger macro-fiscal management

insights.claim: Coalitions of borrower countries pooling analytical resources, building common reporting standards, and engaging rating agencies as a group would have far larger effect on cost of capital than individual finance ministries acting alone.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Watch for a borrowers' cartel-style ratings engagement bloc as a new institutional actor in EM sovereign credit.
insights.locator: Although individual action is making a difference

insights.claim: Fiscal reform compounds: lower leakage improves fiscal capacity, stronger fiscal capacity improves creditworthiness, and lower financing costs free up more room for development investment.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: The payoff to governance improvement is nonlinear, which favors early-mover reformer sovereigns over the index.
insights.locator: These efforts reinforce each other

insights.claim: Donors should route more grant funding into multilateral replenishments such as the International Development Association, regional development bank concession funds, the Green Climate Fund, and the major global health funds, because these pool contributions with reflows from earlier lending, market borrowing, and existing fiduciary systems.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Replenishment outcomes for IDA and the Green Climate Fund become the key observable for whether the system consolidates or keeps fragmenting.
insights.locator: Boost grant funding in multilateral replenishments

insights.claim: Pooled funding is irreplaceable for cross-border public goods — climate mitigation, pandemic preparedness, and regional stability — whose benefits fall outside the country making the investment, so no individual donor has an incentive to finance them alone.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: The bilateral turn systematically underfunds pandemic and climate resilience — a mispriced global tail risk.
insights.locator: Pooled aid remains essential for basic services

insights.claim: Using every remaining grant dollar to mobilize private investment would push scarce grants toward return-generating activities and away from fragile states, vulnerable populations, and services that cannot support repayment.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: The prevailing mobilization-ratio metric is the wrong KPI; it quietly defunds the hardest cases while looking efficient.
insights.quote: Anything more risks transferring public subsidy to private investors without producing additional development impact.
insights.locator: Protect grants as a primary vehicle and deploy catalytic capital judiciously

insights.claim: The correct test for concessional capital is whether the funding actually changes the investment decision and how little concessionality is required to do so — anything beyond that is a subsidy transfer to private investors.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: A usable diligence screen for impact and blended-finance allocators: measure minimum-viable concessionality, not deal volume.
insights.quote: The test is whether the funding changes the investment decision and how little concessionality is needed to do so.
insights.locator: Where private investment is viable

insights.claim: Some concessional money goes unused because grant, philanthropic, impact, and multilateral funds are scattered across innumerable institutions and recipients cannot see where the money sits or afford the application and compliance costs; a global registry plus AI-based matching and standardized sector templates would address that search-and-access cost directly.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Discovery and compliance friction — not just volume — is a binding constraint, creating a niche for infrastructure that matches projects to capital.
insights.locator: Make concessional capital easier to find and cheaper to access

insights.claim: Multilateral coordination efforts like the Lusaka Agenda, which seeks strategic and operational coherence among global health initiatives, should be strengthened and replicated across the broader development finance ecosystem because recipient governments still manage dozens of funders with separate cycles and reporting.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Coordination architecture is the cheapest available source of effective funding increase when nominal volumes are falling.
insights.locator: Greater reliance on multilateral channels, however

themes.theme: DFI Market-Building and MDB Balance Sheets

insights.claim: Bilateral development finance institutions should identify the parts of health, education, and climate investment that can carry commercial, semi-commercial, or lightly concessional capital, so grants can concentrate on the systems that genuinely cannot support a return.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Social-sector market creation is where new investable pipeline will be manufactured — an emerging opportunity set for impact-oriented capital.
insights.locator: Enable market creation in the social sectors

insights.claim: The sector's persistent preference for first-ever, innovative transactions over standardized, repeatable capital stacks destroys value, because a replicable deal is worth far more than a novel one that cannot be replayed.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Scalability, not novelty, is the screening criterion for development deal structures — a direct critique of how blended finance is currently marketed.
insights.quote: A replicable deal is far more valuable than one that is innovative but difficult to replay.
insights.locator: Standardize repeatable capital stacks and structures

insights.claim: Bilateral institutions partnering with public development banks and local financial institutions — providing longer tenors, absorbing early risk, or offering limited concession while a market develops — can hand the market to domestic capital once the performance record is clear.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: Domestic financial institutions in emerging markets become the eventual holders of de-risked development assets — a channel for local capital market deepening.
insights.locator: Team up with public development banks (PDBs)

insights.claim: Multilateral development bank boards should explicitly quantify the development impact forgone by preserving a triple-A rating, since a AAA rating is a tool of the development mandate rather than the mandate itself.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: A live policy debate that could unlock meaningful incremental MDB lending capacity — and reprice MDB bonds if boards ever act on it.
insights.quote: Indeed, this is an essential component of the MDB value proposition and is a powerful tool of the development mandate, but it is not the mandate itself. Development impact is the mandate.
insights.locator: Calculate the foregone development impact of preserving top credit ratings

insights.claim: Some low- and middle-income sovereign borrowers face rates of 10% to 13% in global capital markets, so a multilateral development bank borrowing at AA+ instead of AAA could still lend on far better terms than the alternative.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: The cost-benefit arithmetic of a one-notch MDB downgrade is far more favorable than the sector's rating orthodoxy assumes — a potential structural supply increase in concessional-adjacent lending.
insights.quote: Some low- and middle-income sovereign borrowers face rates of 10% to 13% in global capital markets.
insights.locator: How much would a rating change increase the bank’s own cost of capital?

insights.claim: Multilateral development banks cannot know their true prudential lending limit while staying safely inside it, so they should model more ambitious lending scenarios, move toward the boundary, and prepare snap-back strategies through lending, capital, or portfolio management in case a rating threshold is crossed.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: If boards adopt this, MDB lending headroom becomes a policy variable rather than a fixed constraint — watch capital-adequacy reform follow-through.
insights.quote: An institution can’t really know the limit until it is crossed.
insights.locator: Test lending boundaries through scenario modeling

insights.claim: Lower traditional aid volumes need not mean less development, but only if leaders assemble the right mix of providers, instruments, and terms around each specific need rather than treating the old system as recoverable.
insights.speaker: BCG Henderson Institute
insights.so_what: The framing to adopt when evaluating development-finance institutions: judge them on instrument-matching capability, not on how much aid they replaced.
insights.quote: Lower levels of traditional forms of aid do not have to mean less development. Rather, this reduced aid demands a fundamentally different financial system.
insights.locator: In the new development aid system, success will depend
